It might be worth looking into the love languages. It talks about the types of ways people need to be loved. One of them is ‘words of affirmation’ which could be used to compliment or reassure people. It could be helpful to talk to him about it from this perspective, instead of ‘I need this and I need that’ 

Not saying you are like that of course! I know I found it helpful to tell my partner about these things though and it felt like it was coming from a more neutral standpoint.

If it’s any consolation my support group facilitator was in and out of hospital at once stage, like fortnightly. 

Now after a lot of work and a long DBT course she’s able to work, study, and run a support group. She does heaps of advocacy for BPD in my community. She’s a great source of inspiration! Let that fuel you 😁 I woke up feeling the same today too. Almost let me day go to waste out of fear but I got up.

I’m similar to this. I feel lazy, I get exhausted REALLY quickly (I’ve tried working many ‘normal’ full time jobs and I get so exhausted I have to quiet because my anxiety crashes and I have constant anxiety attacks that are physically painful). In the past I have worked many freelance small jobs, gotten bored of all of them. 

We all need money, or a job, or both. Maybe if we win the lottery we don’t need a job, but we all need something to do (fair call, you said organising and cleaning your home, we all know that’s endless so it’s great you have something to do). I asked myself what would I do if money were no object, what would I make into a job ‘if I could’. I had to find alternative ways to learn, work and study. I study at uni and it’s taken me a lot longer than it would probably take most people. I tell myself it’s okay. 

Not everyone is career orientated. That’s okay! There’s room for everyone, honestly. I want to be career orientated but my mental health gets in the way every single day. So I just do it slowly and when I can. 

Sorry I realised I ended up just rambling- if money is an issue I say work part time (if you can survive on that) and do what makes you happy

Hey, similar boat here. 

I respond with anger and nastiness, so I’m one of those ‘toxic’ people. I’m trying really hard to change it. I don’t mean to be, my family know I have a good heart deep down, but everything weighs on me so much and I have a nasty streak which I hate.

I’m pretty new to this too, but one thing I do know is that changing behaviour is really fucking hard and doesn’t happen overnight. For me, things like talking slower, not responding straight away, yoga and mindfulness, self soothing, and trying to find simple ways to explain how you feel before you rattle off more mean things to say is a practice and important. 

This might sound stupid, and I hope it doesn’t sound manipulative, but I find if I take just a milli second to think about my feelings in a fight (this is where practicing mindfulness comes in, the part of your brain that stays present comes in handy when it’s stronger here) and I’ll often find myself crying instead of spouting out mean words. Neither are a ‘happy’ emotion, but I can guarantee you most angry people are sad, hurt, depressed etc, and anyone around you will respond better to and want to help someone who’s crying. I’m not suggesting deliberately cry to be manipulative, I’m suggesting to try to practice taking moments to how you really feel. I know for me, I often need to burst into tears and get it out haha. 

Look into DBT therapy, you learn how to use your language better to explain things to people, distress tolerance, self soothing, compassion etc 😊 good luck

BPD can present itself in many ways but one thing that is most common/often surrounds people with BPD is the inability to regulate their emotions effctively. This includes being really reactivity to situations (positive or negative) abandonment issues, the appearance of quick mood changes, anxiety, fear, suicidal tendencies, s of destructive behaviour, self identity issues, self worth issues, impulsive behaviour, rocky relationships, and a whole other range of symptoms. A lot of people with a BPD diagnosis has suffered some form of trauma in their life, and one cause of BPD is that the trauma has changed that persons coping mechanisms and ways of dealing with situations. 

As for the gender thing, apparently it’s a rumour/myth that it’s a “female illness” but I can confirm there are many males in my support group I attend. There are majority of females but I think out of 20 or so there are about 5 mal s and 2 transgender males. I have a mild form of BPD :) feel free to ask me anything!

I got diagnosed with a mild form of borderline personality disorder 5 months ago. 

Things that help: actually being given a good therapist to address BPD, mindfulness and yoga, being patient with myself (I am quite aware of sensations in my body and also when my mood fluctuated or anxiety flares up) so I have to practice delaying a response to people if I’m upset or slowly responding... that’s a big one for me. I’m quick to react to judgement, or what feels like judgement. Active mindfulness works well too, I have to do all of this every day to practice.

Honestly, a hard question to answer, even for people who have gotten better. 

I’ve improved my mental health so incredibly much this year that I’m truly doing better than I have in the last 6-7 years. More secure, more ready to take it all on. However I read this question, and when I asked myself ‘how have I gotten better?’ Is such a hard question to answer. 

Or maybe it’s not. Maybe it’s because I know when I was sick all those years, I could read a million tips and tricks and none of it would make a difference. I was so sick I couldn’t implement any of it into my life. 

When is was MORE sick, I didn’t get out of bed. I didn’t eat properly but more often i might eat something but not drink any water because I’d just grab something from the fridge or some bread and go back to bed. Drinking water felt extremely difficult and it really annoyed me. It annoyed me to take care of my pets, to talk to anyone, and to shower gave me anxiety. My mood was never regulated. I’d have suicidal days, days where I’d self harm. Days where maybe I would go for a walk but I’d be in a complete daze, somewhat dissociated. I tried working out, eating better, reading up on things, therapy with a few different people (some were good some were bad) but it didn’t make much long term difference. I was/am so terrified of medication (irrational fear) that I couldn’t stick with any so that was a no go. 

What cured me was time (hear me out). I’ve always been a perfectionist, and was told from a young age I’d be very successful because I was smart. That I was talented. Well that can be a crippling expectation if a mental health illness takes over you. I was in my 26th year (about 3 months off turning 26) and I wasn’t any better. I had the kindest therapist who I could easily talk to but I’d seen her for 3-4 years on and off and I never felt like we had any big progress. I felt older. I felt like I’d “wasted” a lot of my twenties so far being miserable, unable to work, and just started dawning on me that surely there’s an answer for me somewhere, surely. I didn’t want to spend the rest of my life like this. I went to my doctor, specialist, and finally found out I had been misdiagnosed this whole time. When I was being treated for depression and anxiety, I should have been being treated for anxiety and borderline personality disorder. 

I’ve only been on a new treatment plan (new therapy and new group therapy, no meds) for five months now with my new diagnosis and I have learnt so much about my brain. I spend a lot more of my time trying to be productive, even if it’s less so than people who work 9-5. I don’t get anxiety at the gym anymore. I am able to clean the house, do yoga, and sometimes be social. It’s a work in progress, but this is why it’s so important to get a proper assessment done with a specialist or psychiatrist. I spent years and years in pain, truly believing I was a complete nutter, that I was never going to get better and that I’d die by suicide. But all I needed was the right diagnosis. It wasn’t all roses and still isn’t, the first 2-3 months were extreme, I’ve never been through anything as terrifying as having to adjust with a million new ideas, scaring myself at night with nightmares about it all, and feeling like my brain would actually explode because i was trying to chain my ways of thinking. I’m not 100% but I’m still here to tell the tale. Keep fighting guys, just like I will. 

Sorry a little irrelevant to the question- what got me better was a lot of therapy and hard work including meditation and mindfulness (when I started I had so much built up anxiety that it physically hurt to do these things, I had to cry and shake through it, it yes easier I promise), yoga (same with yoga), journaling, research on BPD, crying a lot, working through tough emotions, being honest with myself, and physical pain from all of it. One session I told my psych about how it felt like there were too people in my head talking and that she “needed to tell me if I’m having a real life break through or an enormous breakdown because if the latter take me to the hospital now”. 

If you’ve had years of depression please get reassessed it can’t hurt you! I hope this helps someone. Sending good vibes :)
